questions.passage: The mural project took three months. Art teacher Mr. Jackson sketched the design, and students painted after school. The mural, which depicts local plants and animals, [and it brightens the east wall of the gym]. Visitors often stop to take photos of it.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: brightening the east wall of the gym
and it brightens the east wall of the gym
brightens the east wall of the gym
which brightens the east wall of the gym
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a main verb after the nonrestrictive description of the mural. Brightens makes the mural the subject of a complete main clause, while and it brightens creates a compound predicate without a main verb before the conjunction. Brightening leaves the sentence without a finite verb, and which brightens adds another dependent clause while still leaving the main clause incomplete.

questions.passage: The student council is turning an unused courtyard into a lunchtime garden. [Students will be able to eat at picnic tables surrounded by herbs and flowers.] The council plans to recruit volunteers for watering and weeding. It also hopes to install a small stage for open-mic performances. The garden should give students a pleasant place to relax between classes.
questions.q: The writer is considering deleting the bracketed sentence. Should the writer keep or delete that sentence?
options: Delete it, because picnic tables and flowers are not mentioned elsewhere in the paragraph.
Delete it, because the paragraph does not explain who will water the plants.
Keep it, because it describes a benefit of the new garden and supports the paragraph's focus on the courtyard project.
Keep it, because it identifies the volunteers who will care for the garden.
questions.explanation: The sentence explains one way students will use the redesigned courtyard, so it directly supports the paragraph's focus on the garden as a student space. The other reasons for deleting do not address whether the sentence contributes to that focus. The sentence also does not identify the volunteers, so that reason for keeping it is inaccurate.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The debate team has revised its schedule to allow more practice time. [Each of the captains have agreed to lead one extra session per week]. These sessions will focus on rebuttals and cross-examination. The team hopes the added practice will help it qualify for the state tournament.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: Each of the captains have agreed to lead one extra sessions per week
Each of the captain has agreed to lead one extra session per week
Each of the captains has agreed to lead one extra session per week
Each of the captains have agreed to lead one extra session per week
questions.explanation: The subject of the clause is Each, which is singular, so it requires the singular verb has agreed. The phrase of the captains does not change the subject's number, and captains should remain plural after of. The version with one extra sessions also has an agreement error between one and sessions.

questions.passage: The after-school culinary club at Lincoln High meets twice a week. Members plan menus, measure ingredients, and practice safe knife techniques. They also learn how to keep a kitchen clean and how to budget for groceries. At the end of each month, the club serves lunch to teachers and families. [The club has become popular with students.]
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the writer's goal of emphasizing the practical skills students learn in the culinary club?
options: Teachers and families enjoy the monthly lunches.
Many members joined because their friends did.
By the end of the term, members can prepare a meal and manage a kitchen more independently.
The club meets in the school kitchen on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
questions.explanation: The goal is to emphasize practical skills, and the sentence about preparing meals and managing a kitchen more independently summarizes the useful abilities developed through the club's activities. The options about joining with friends, meeting times, and monthly lunches focus on social reasons, scheduling, or audience reactions instead of skills. The correct sentence fits after the details about planning menus, measuring, knife safety, cleaning, and budgeting.

questions.passage: The town council voted to extend the walking trail through the old rail yard. The plan includes several benches and a small overlook[, it will also connect the east side of town to the riverfront]. Construction is scheduled to begin next summer.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: it will also connect the east side of town to the riverfront
; it will also connect the east side of town to the riverfront
, will also connect the east side of town to the riverfront
, it will also connect the east side of town to the riverfront
questions.explanation: The bracketed portion contains a second independent clause, so a semicolon is needed to separate it from the first independent clause. A comma alone creates a comma splice, omitting the subject in the next clause makes it incomplete, and leaving no punctuation creates a run-on. The semicolon keeps the two closely related statements correctly joined.

questions.passage: Many residents need tools for small home repairs but cannot afford to buy them. The new tool library on Oak Street lets people borrow drills, ladders, and saws for free. Members check out tools with a library card and return them within one week. [The library also offers workshops on basic repairs.] Because the workshops fill quickly, people are encouraged to register early.
questions.q: The writer is considering moving the bracketed sentence. Where would it best be placed?
options: After the sentence about how quickly the workshops fill.
At the end of the paragraph, after the sentence encouraging early registration.
At the start of the paragraph, before the explanation of why residents need tools.
Immediately before the sentence about how quickly the workshops fill.
questions.explanation: The bracketed sentence introduces the workshops, and the following sentence explains that those workshops fill quickly and require early registration. Placing the introductory sentence immediately before the sentence about filling quickly gives the clearest cause-and-effect flow. Moving it earlier would interrupt the explanation of borrowing tools, and moving it later would make the reference to workshops occur before the sentence that introduces them.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The robotics team spent months designing a robot that could sort recyclable materials. [Neither the coach nor the students was sure that the robot would work at the competition]. During the first round, the robot dropped a plastic bottle but recovered quickly. The team's careful testing paid off when the robot finished in second place.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: Neither the coach nor the students was sure that the robot would work at the competition
Neither the coach nor the students were sure that the robot would work at the competition
The coach nor the students were sure that the robot would work at the competition
Neither the coach or the students were sure that the robot would work at the competition
questions.explanation: With a neither . . . nor construction, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it; students is plural, so were is correct. The original was is singular and therefore does not agree with students. The other choices either omit neither or use or instead of nor in the paired construction.

questions.passage: Last year, a group of neighbors noticed that the empty lot on Pine Street was collecting trash. They organized monthly cleanups, planted native grasses, and added two benches. Local businesses donated materials, and the city installed a path. [The lot has become a useful community space.] Now families use the area for picnics, and students walk through it on their way to school.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to state the main point of the paragraph?
options: Families enjoy picnicking near native grasses and benches.
Local businesses are often asked to donate materials for city projects.
By working together, neighbors turned a neglected lot into a shared community space.
The empty lot on Pine Street was once used for storing construction materials.
questions.explanation: The paragraph describes neighbors, businesses, and the city cooperating to improve an empty lot that residents now use, so the sentence about turning a neglected lot into a shared community space captures the main point. The detail about picnicking is only one supporting example, while the statements about construction materials and donations from businesses are either unsupported or too narrow. The correct sentence summarizes the overall change described in the paragraph.

questions.passage: The debate team at Riverside High has been preparing for the statewide tournament since January. To prepare for the statewide debate tournament, [the team reviewed videos of past matches, practiced rebuttals, and Ms. Chen organized mock rounds]. The extra work helped them respond more confidently to unexpected arguments. Their coach said the team's improvement was noticeable in the final scrimmage.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: the team reviewed videos of past matches, practiced rebuttals, and participated in mock rounds organized by Ms. Chen
the team reviewed videos of past matches, practiced rebuttals, and mock rounds were organized by Ms. Chen
the team reviewed videos of past matches, practiced rebuttals, and Ms. Chen's organizing mock rounds
the team reviewed videos of past matches, practiced rebuttals, and Ms. Chen organized mock rounds
questions.explanation: The list should use parallel past-tense verbs for actions performed by the team: reviewed, practiced, and participated. The original shifts to a new subject, Ms. Chen, in the middle of the list, and the other choices also break the parallel structure with a passive clause or a noun phrase. Participated in mock rounds organized by Ms. Chen keeps the focus on the team's preparations and completes the list correctly.

questions.passage: The city’s new teen center, [designed by Maya Ruiz, and paid for with a $2.5 million grant], opened on Saturday. Students toured the recording studio, the study lounge, and the art room. The center will offer free after-school programs and a homework help desk.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the bracketed portion?
options: designed by Maya Ruiz; and paid for with a $2.5 million grant
designed by Maya Ruiz and paid for with a $2.5 million grant
designed by Maya Ruiz and paid for, with a $2.5 million grant
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The phrase set off by commas is a nonessential modifier made of two participial phrases joined by 'and,' so no comma belongs before 'and.' The semicolon wrongly breaks the modifier, and the comma before 'with' separates 'paid for' from its prepositional phrase.

questions.passage: The collection of essays [were edited by Dr. Chen and published in a student journal]. It includes work by twelve seniors. The journal will be sold at the campus bookstore for $8, and proceeds will fund next year’s writing contest.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: was edited by Dr. Chen and published in a student journal
were edited by Dr. Chen and was published in a student journal
NO CHANGE
was edited by Dr. Chen and publishing in a student journal
questions.explanation: The subject is 'collection,' which is singular, so the verb must be 'was edited.' The compound passive 'was edited ... and published ...' is parallel and complete, while the other choices create agreement or parallelism errors.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: The intersection near Lincoln Elementary is dangerous. [A bunch of kids have almost gotten hit there], and parents are worried. The city should install a crosswalk with flashing lights before the start of the school year. Similar crossings in neighboring towns have reduced accidents.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to maintain a formal, professional tone?
options: Plenty of children have almost gotten hit there
NO CHANGE
Several students have nearly been struck there
A bunch of students have nearly been hit there
questions.explanation: 'Several students have nearly been struck there' uses neutral, precise wording suitable for a professional letter. The casual words 'bunch,' 'kids,' and 'gotten hit' make the other choices too informal for this tone.

questions.passage: The awards committee recognized three student scientists: [Luis Ortega, a chemistry major, Maya Chen, a biology major, and Jamal Wright, a math major]. Each received a $500 scholarship and a certificate at the spring banquet. Their research projects will be displayed in the library through May.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the list in the bracketed portion?
options: Luis Ortega; a chemistry major, Maya Chen; a biology major, and Jamal Wright; a math major
Luis Ortega, a chemistry major; Maya Chen, a biology major; and Jamal Wright, a math major
NO CHANGE
Luis Ortega, a chemistry major; Maya Chen; a biology major, and Jamal Wright, a math major
questions.explanation: Each item in the list contains an internal comma that sets off the person's field of study, so the main items must be separated by semicolons. The commas-only version blurs the boundaries between the three people. The other choices misplace semicolons within the items.

questions.passage: Walking into the gym, [the new mural surprised the students]. Its bright colors depicted local athletes and landmarks. The art club spent six weeks designing and painting it after school. The principal said the mural was the club’s most ambitious project yet.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: surprising the students, the new mural
NO CHANGE
the new mural was surprising to the students
the students were surprised by the new mural
questions.explanation: The opening phrase 'Walking into the gym' describes the students, so the main clause must begin with 'the students.' The other choices leave the mural as the one walking, creating a dangling modifier.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: The mayor’s proposal would [make the city’s recycling program bigger] by adding two new collection routes and a second sorting facility. Supporters say the change could reduce landfill waste by 15 percent. The city council will vote on the plan next month.
questions.q: Which choice best expresses the writer’s meaning with precise, formal language?
options: NO CHANGE
expand the city’s recycling program
enlarge the city’s recycling program’s size
grow the city’s recycling program up
questions.explanation: 'Expand' is the precise, formal verb for increasing a program's scope, and it fits idiomatically with 'program.' 'Make bigger,' 'grow up,' and 'enlarge the size' are either informal, unidiomatic, or redundant.

questions.passage: The science club’s annual report, [which summarizes the group’s experiments was posted online yesterday]. It includes data from more than 200 students and a list of upcoming projects. Club members will present the report at the next school board meeting.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the bracketed portion?
options: which summarizes the group’s experiments; was posted online yesterday
which summarizes the group’s experiments, was posted online, yesterday
which summarizes the group’s experiments, was posted online yesterday
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The clause beginning with 'which' is nonessential and must be closed with a comma before the main verb 'was posted.' A semicolon cannot separate the nonessential clause from the main verb, and no comma is needed before 'yesterday.'

questions.passage: To prepare for the statewide debate tournament, [the team practiced rebuttals every afternoon and reviewing case files with Coach Alvarez]. The extra work paid off when the team advanced to the semifinals. Coach Alvarez said the students’ preparation and teamwork made the difference.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: practicing rebuttals every afternoon and reviewing case files with Coach Alvarez
the team practicing rebuttals every afternoon and reviewing case files with Coach Alvarez
NO CHANGE
the team practiced rebuttals every afternoon and reviewed case files with Coach Alvarez
questions.explanation: The sentence needs parallel past-tense verbs after 'the team': 'practiced' and 'reviewed.' The forms with 'reviewing' or 'practicing' break parallelism or leave the sentence without a main verb.

questions.passage: The regional robotics finals took place in Austin, Texas, [on March 8 2025]. The host school provided tables, power strips, and a practice arena. Judges reviewed each team’s design notebook and interviewed students about their build process. The top two teams advanced to the state competition.
questions.q: Which version of the bracketed date is correct in standard written English?
options: on March 8, 2025,
on March 8, 2025
on March, 8 2025
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: In American usage, a comma separates the day from the year: March 8, 2025. The unchanged version lacks that comma, while placing a comma after March or an extra comma before the period misplaces punctuation.

questions.passage: Ms. Okafor’s chemistry class designed water filters from sand, gravel, and charcoal [the students then tested each filter with three samples of creek water]. The clearest sample came from a filter built by a team led by Nash and Priya. Although the prototype was simple, it removed most visible sediment.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion so that the two clauses are joined correctly?
options: and the students, then tested each filter with three samples of creek water
, the students then tested each filter with three samples of creek water
; the students then tested each filter with three samples of creek water
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The material before the bracket and the bracketed clause are both independent clauses, so a semicolon correctly separates them. A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation runs the clauses together.

questions.passage: The volunteer coordinators assigned three teams [students from Lincoln High, who handled registration; parents and teachers, who managed the food tables; and local business owners, who provided supplies]. Each team wore a different color badge, and all volunteers attended a short training session before the event began.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to punctuate the series correctly?
options: students from Lincoln High; who handled registration, parents and teachers; who managed the food tables, and local business owners; who provided supplies
NO CHANGE
: students from Lincoln High, who handled registration; parents and teachers, who managed the food tables; and local business owners, who provided supplies
students from Lincoln High, who handled registration, parents and teachers, who managed the food tables, and local business owners, who provided supplies
questions.explanation: A colon introduces the list of three teams, and semicolons separate the items because each item contains a comma with its who clause. The unchanged version lacks the introducing colon, and replacing semicolons with commas would confuse the list’s internal punctuation.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The robotics club at Eastgate High School [has] spent months designing a lightweight arm for its competition robot. Each of the team’s four subgroups has a different job: one builds the frame, another wires the motors, a third programs the controls, and the fourth tests every joint. At the regional contest, the team hopes to qualify for the state finals.
questions.q: Which choice best completes the sentence logically and grammatically?
options: have
are having
has
having
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun club, not the plural word robotics, so the singular verb has is required. The version with have makes the subject and verb disagree, and having would leave the sentence without a finite main verb.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: During the debate about later school start times, Mr. Delgado asked [my sister and I] to summarize the survey results for the school board. The board members listened closely, especially to the data about sleep and attendance. After the meeting, they thanked us for presenting the information so clearly.
questions.q: For the bracketed portion, which choice is grammatically correct?
options: I and my sister
my sister and myself
my sister and me
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of asked, so the objective case me is required in the compound object my sister and me. The subject form I, as in the unchanged version, is a common overcorrection; the reflexive myself also has no clear antecedent and does not fit here.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: At Monday’s meeting, the city council discussed a proposal to add bike lanes along Oak Avenue. The plan [got a lot of angry feedback] from some drivers who worried about losing parking spaces. Supporters, however, argued that safer routes would help students bike to school and reduce traffic near the library.
questions.q: Which choice is the most precise and formal replacement for the bracketed portion?
options: drew considerable criticism
made a bunch of drivers mad
NO CHANGE
was hit by a storm of negative vibes
questions.explanation: The council’s response needs a concise, formal phrase, and drew considerable criticism expresses the idea without informal wording. The unchanged phrase and the slangy alternatives are too casual or vague for a public meeting report.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: Dear Principal Alvarez, I am writing on behalf of the Cooking for Community Club. We meet on Wednesdays and prepare meals for a local shelter, but our current kitchen space is too small for the growing number of members. I am [bugging you about letting us use the cafeteria after school on Fridays] so we can prepare more meals. Thank you for considering our request.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to maintain a respectful tone in the letter?
options: wondering if you could maybe, like, let the club use the cafeteria after school on Fridays
demanding that you allow the club to use the cafeteria after school on Fridays
writing to ask whether the club may use the cafeteria after school on Fridays
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The letter should make a polite request, so writing to ask whether the club may use the cafeteria conveys the request respectfully. The unchanged wording is too casual, while demanding is rude and the maybe, like wording is informal.

questions.passage: Last spring, students at Riverside Middle School turned a weedy lot behind the gym into a vegetable garden. Science classes now use the space to test soil pH and track plant growth. [Add a sentence here.] The garden also supplies tomatoes, peppers, and herbs to the school cafeteria. Teachers hope to add a small greenhouse next year so seedlings can be started earlier.
questions.q: The writer wants to add a sentence after the second sentence that explains how the garden provides hands-on science lessons. Which sentence best accomplishes that goal?
options: The lot was once covered with weeds and broken glass.
For example, students compare how plants grow in sun and shade and record their observations in science journals.
The cafeteria uses the vegetables in salads and soups throughout the fall.
A local nursery donated seed packets and gardening gloves.
questions.explanation: The goal is to explain how the garden provides hands-on science lessons, so a sentence about students comparing plant growth in sun and shade and recording observations directly supports that point. The other sentences concern cafeteria use, the lot’s history, or donated supplies rather than science lessons.

questions.passage: At the Westside Community Center, the new tool library lends equipment to residents for free. Members can borrow up to three items at a time, and they must return each item on the due date printed on their receipt. [The center also hosts a summer basketball league in its gym.] Volunteers inspect every returned tool and make minor repairs before the item goes back on the shelf. Since opening in January, the library has lent more than four hundred tools, from hammers to hedge trimmers.
questions.q: The writer wants to keep the paragraph focused on the tool library. Which choice best indicates what should be done with the bracketed sentence?
options: Delete it because it shifts the paragraph away from the tool library.
Keep it because it shows that the center serves many residents.
Move it to the beginning of the paragraph to describe the center’s programs.
Keep it because it explains how residents learn about the tool library.
questions.explanation: The paragraph’s focus is the tool library, and the basketball league does not help explain how the library serves residents. Deleting the sentence keeps the paragraph coherent and on topic; keeping or moving it would introduce an unrelated program.

questions.passage: Every Thursday evening, the Oakdale Community Kitchen offers a free cooking class for families. Participants learn to prepare low-cost meals using ingredients available at the nearby food pantry. At the end of each session, everyone receives a recipe card and a bag of groceries. Since the program began, more than two hundred families have attended, and many have started cooking together at home. [Add a concluding sentence here.]
questions.q: The writer wants to conclude the paragraph by emphasizing the program’s growth. Which sentence best replaces the bracketed text?
options: The kitchen is located on Oak Street, near the public library.
As word spread, the class expanded from one table to three and now includes families from across the neighborhood.
Many people enjoy cooking at home.
The recipe cards include dishes from several countries.
questions.explanation: To emphasize growth, the concluding sentence should show the class expanding in size or reach. The sentence about expanding from one table to three and drawing families from across the neighborhood does that; the location, general enjoyment, and recipe-origin details do not focus on growth.

questions.passage: Last spring, the environmental club at Lincoln High School planted a rain garden beside the parking lot. [The garden absorbs runoff during storms, it also provides habitat for pollinators.] Students now maintain the garden and track which plants attract the most bees.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: The garden absorbs runoff during storms and also provides habitat for pollinators.
NO CHANGE
The garden absorbs runoff during storms; also provides habitat for pollinators.
The garden absorbs runoff during storms. Also providing habitat for pollinators.
questions.explanation: The comma between two complete ideas creates a comma splice; joining the two predicates with the conjunction and fixes the sentence. The semicolon version lacks a subject after the semicolon, and the period version turns the second part into a fragment. The original comma splice is not acceptable.

questions.passage: Maya volunteered to report on the city council's budget for the student newspaper. After reviewing the council's proposed budget, [the new youth center's funding remained unclear to Maya.] She scheduled an interview with the council member who oversees community programs.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: Maya remained unsure about the funding for the new youth center.
the funding for the new youth center remained unclear.
funding for the new youth center was still unclear after Maya reviewed it.
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase describes Maya reviewing the budget, so the main clause must begin with Maya as its subject. The original and the versions beginning with funding leave the modifier dangling. Recasting the clause as Maya remained unsure gives the opening phrase a logical subject.

questions.passage: At the regional science fair, three students from Eastview High School presented a device that measures water waste. [The device attaches to a showerhead it sounds an alert when the shower has run for five minutes.] The students hope to make the alert adjustable for different households.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
The device attaches to a showerhead, it sounds an alert when the shower has run for five minutes.
The device attaches to a showerhead; sounds an alert when the shower has run for five minutes.
The device attaches to a showerhead and sounds an alert when the shower has run for five minutes.
questions.explanation: The original is a run-on because two independent clauses are placed back to back with no connector. Using and joins the two verbs that share the subject The device, producing a complete and correctly punctuated sentence. The comma splice and the semicolon followed by a verb without a subject are both incorrect.

questions.passage: Every Friday, the community kitchen at Riverside High School turns surplus cafeteria ingredients into meals for local families. Student volunteers chop vegetables, package portions, and deliver the meals with adult drivers. [The program began three years ago with only six volunteers.] Now more than forty students participate each week, and the kitchen serves nearly two hundred meals every month.
questions.q: The writer is considering deleting the bracketed sentence. Should the writer keep or delete that sentence?
options: Delete it because it interrupts the description of how volunteers prepare and deliver meals.
Keep it because it explains why students volunteer at the kitchen.
Delete it because it provides no information about the program's current size.
Keep it because it helps show how much the program has grown.
questions.explanation: The sentence tells when the program began and how few volunteers it had, which sets up the contrast with the current forty students and two hundred meals. That contrast makes the program's growth clear, so the sentence contributes to the paragraph's focus. It does not explain why students volunteer.

questions.passage: The student art club spent two months designing a mural for the town's new recreation center. (1) The mural depicts scenes from the town's history, including its early train station and first public library. (2) Club members interviewed longtime residents to gather stories for the design. (3) The recreation center's director asked the artists to include a section about local sports teams. (4) [They then revised their sketches to add this section and submitted the final design for approval.] (5) The finished mural now welcomes visitors in the main hallway.
questions.q: The writer is considering moving the bracketed sentence. Where would it best be placed?
options: After sentence 2
After sentence 3
After sentence 5
After sentence 1
questions.explanation: The pronoun this section refers to the local sports teams section requested by the director, so the sentence must follow the director's request. Placing it after sentence 3 keeps that reference clear and preserves the sequence from request to revision. The other positions either leave this section without a clear referent or place the revision after the finished mural is described.

questions.passage: Rosa assumed the coding club's first workshop would run smoothly. [Therefore,] the laptop cart arrived with only half of the chargers needed for the students, a problem that surprised her. By the afternoon, volunteers had borrowed extras, and every station was ready.
questions.q: Which choice best introduces the second sentence?
options: Therefore,
For instance,
In addition,
However,
questions.explanation: The second sentence presents an unexpected problem, which contrasts with Rosa's assumption that the workshop would run smoothly. However signals that contrast. Therefore would incorrectly suggest that the smooth assumption caused the charger shortage, while the other transitions do not fit the relationship.

questions.passage: Each fall, the robotics club at Crestview High School builds a competition robot from a standard kit. Students design the frame, solder circuit boards, and program the robot to complete specific tasks. [The club meets in the school's technology lab every Tuesday and Thursday.] Members also practice troubleshooting when sensors fail, a skill they will use in many future jobs.
questions.q: The writer wants to emphasize the practical skills students learn in the robotics club. Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: Many members enjoy the annual regional competition.
The technology lab was renovated last summer.
The club's adviser has coached robotics for nearly a decade.
Students learn to use multimeters and power tools safely.
questions.explanation: The sentence about learning to use multimeters and power tools safely names hands-on skills that students can apply beyond the club. The other choices focus on the adviser's experience, students' enjoyment, or the facility, none of which directly emphasizes practical skills learned by students.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The new exhibit at the Fairview Historical Society explores the experiences of immigrant families. The collection of photographs and letters [were donated] by local residents last spring. Curators have arranged the items by decade, allowing visitors to trace how the neighborhood changed over time.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
was donated
are donating
have been donated
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun collection, not the plural nouns photographs and letters, so the verb must be singular. Was donated correctly agrees with collection and fits the past-time phrase last spring. The plural forms do not agree, and are donating wrongly suggests the collection is doing the donating.

questions.passage: At the city’s annual science fair, my teammate Lena and I presented a model of a solar-powered water filter. [The contest’s three judges, who had reviewed more than sixty projects that morning, asked] several detailed questions about our design. We explained how the filter used gravel, sand, and charcoal to remove impurities. By the end of the afternoon, we had earned second place and a $150 award.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the bracketed portion?
options: The contest’s three judges, who had reviewed more than sixty projects that morning, asked
The contest’s three judges who had reviewed more than sixty projects that morning asked
The contest’s three judges, who had reviewed more than sixty projects that morning asked
The contest’s three judges who had reviewed more than sixty projects that morning, asked
questions.explanation: The clause beginning with “who” gives extra information about the judges and is not essential to identify them, so it should be set off by commas on both sides. Removing that clause still leaves the complete sentence “The contest’s three judges asked several detailed questions.” The other choices omit one or both commas and either blur the nonessential clause or create faulty punctuation.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: Dear Ms. Alvarez, Thank you for considering me for the summer internship at your accounting firm. I am eager to learn how a professional office operates. [I think your company is really cool, and I’d love to get a chance to work there.] I have attached my résumé and completed application. I would appreciate the opportunity to discuss my qualifications with you. Sincerely, Nathan Chen
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to maintain a formal, professional tone?
options: I think your company is really cool, and I’d love to get a chance to work there.
I am super excited about your firm and hope you pick me for the internship.
I admire your firm’s reputation and would welcome the opportunity to contribute to its team.
Your company is awesome, and working there would be a dream come true.
questions.explanation: The sentence about admiring the firm’s reputation and welcoming an opportunity to contribute uses respectful, professional wording appropriate for a letter to an employer. The original and the other choices rely on casual words such as “cool,” “awesome,” and “super,” which do not match the formal tone of the letter.

questions.passage: Marisol had volunteered at the community garden all summer. [She learned how to test soil pH, prune tomato plants, and she also learned to manage a compost bin.] By August, she could identify every vegetable in the garden and explain how each one grew. Her favorite task was teaching younger children how to water the seedlings without damaging their roots.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: She learned how to test soil pH, pruning tomato plants, and to manage a compost bin.
She learned how to test soil pH, prune tomato plants, and manage a compost bin.
She learned how to test soil pH, how to prune tomato plants, and managing a compost bin.
She learned how to test soil pH, prune tomato plants, and she also learned to manage a compost bin.
questions.explanation: The three garden tasks should be expressed in parallel form after “learned how to.” The correct version uses “test,” “prune,” and “manage” as matching verb forms. The original shifts into a new independent clause, while the other choices mix gerund and infinitive forms.

questions.passage: Over spring break, our environmental club collected used sneakers for a recycling program. [The club meets on the first Thursday of every month in Room 204.] We set up collection boxes at the library, the community center, and the high school gym. By the end of the week, we had gathered 312 pairs of shoes, which the program will turn into athletic surfaces for playgrounds. Our adviser, Mr. Okafor, said the project was one of the club’s most successful service efforts.
questions.q: The writer wants to keep the paragraph focused on the sneaker collection project. Should the writer keep or delete the bracketed sentence?
options: Delete it, because it provides information unrelated to the sneaker collection project.
Keep it, because it explains why the club collected sneakers.
Keep it, because it helps readers find the club’s meetings.
Delete it, because it repeats information given earlier in the paragraph.
questions.explanation: The bracketed sentence gives the club’s meeting schedule, which is not connected to the sneaker collection project described in the paragraph. Keeping the paragraph focused on the project means removing that unrelated detail. The sentence does not explain the reason for the collection or repeat earlier information.

questions.passage: The school’s multicultural fair filled the gym with music, food, and student presentations. [Visitors could sample Pakistani biryani, a rice dish with spices, Mexican pan dulce, a sweet bread, and Nigerian jollof rice, a tomato-based rice dish.] Each booth also displayed photographs and maps. At the end of the evening, the student council thanked everyone who had helped make the event a success.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the list in the bracketed portion?
options: Visitors could sample Pakistani biryani, a rice dish with spices; Mexican pan dulce, a sweet bread; and Nigerian jollof rice, a tomato-based rice dish.
Visitors could sample Pakistani biryani, a rice dish with spices; Mexican pan dulce, a sweet bread, and Nigerian jollof rice, a tomato-based rice dish.
Visitors could sample Pakistani biryani; a rice dish with spices; Mexican pan dulce; a sweet bread; and Nigerian jollof rice; a tomato-based rice dish.
Visitors could sample Pakistani biryani, a rice dish with spices, Mexican pan dulce, a sweet bread, and Nigerian jollof rice, a tomato-based rice dish.
questions.explanation: Because each main list item includes a comma-separated description, semicolons are needed between the items to keep the list clear. The correct version separates the three food items with semicolons while keeping each description attached with a comma. The other versions either use only commas or scatter semicolons within the descriptions.

questions.passage: During the robotics competition, Mei noticed that her team’s robot would not move. After checking the wiring and testing the motor, [the problem was still not clear to Mei.] She then replaced the battery pack and tried the controls again. Within minutes, the robot rolled forward and picked up the plastic ball. The team cheered as the judges awarded them a spot in the next round.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: it was still unclear what the problem was to Mei.
the problem was still not clear to Mei.
Mei still could not identify the problem.
the problem still confused Mei.
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase describes Mei’s actions, so the subject of the main clause must be Mei. The original and the other choices make “the problem” or “it” the subject, which wrongly suggests that the problem was checking the wiring and testing the motor. “Mei still could not identify the problem” correctly attaches the action to Mei.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: Our neighborhood library plans to extend its weekend hours, and the staff is asking residents for feedback. At a public meeting, Jamal said, [“I think the longer schedule would be a good thing for students who need a quiet place to study after school.”] The library director noted that many families had requested the change. The new hours will begin next month if the budget is approved.
questions.q: Which choice best expresses Jamal’s idea with precise, formal language?
options: “The longer hours sound kind of nice for kids who want some quiet.”
“Students who need to study after school would probably like it if the library stayed open longer.”
“I think the longer schedule would be a good thing for students who need a quiet place to study after school.”
“The extended schedule would greatly benefit students who need a quiet place to study after school.”
questions.explanation: The correct version replaces the vague phrase “a good thing” with “would greatly benefit,” which states the benefit directly and in a formal way. The original is wordy and informal, while the other choices use colloquial wording such as “kind of nice” or “would probably like it.”

questions.passage: Many towns are turning empty lots into community orchards. First, local officials test the soil to make sure it is safe for growing food. Then residents choose tree varieties that will thrive in the local climate. After several years, the orchards provide shade, beauty, and free fruit. [Volunteers plant the young trees and care for them during their first few years.] The program has become especially popular in neighborhoods where grocery stores are scarce.
questions.q: The writer is considering moving the bracketed sentence. Where would it best be placed?
options: After “The program has become especially popular in neighborhoods where grocery stores are scarce.”
Before “First, local officials test the soil to make sure it is safe for growing food.”
After “Then residents choose tree varieties that will thrive in the local climate.”
Where it is now, after the sentence about the orchards providing shade, beauty, and free fruit.
questions.explanation: The bracketed sentence describes planting, which logically follows choosing tree varieties and comes before the orchards mature enough to provide fruit. Placing it after the sentence about choosing varieties keeps the events in chronological order. The final sentence about the program’s popularity is a concluding point, so putting the planting sentence after it disrupts the sequence.

questions.passage: Last weekend, the Riverside High math club hosted a fundraiser for the local animal shelter. [The students’ goal was to raise enough money to buy new blankets for every dog and cat.] They sold baked goods and raffle tickets outside the grocery store on Main Street. By noon, the club had raised $425. The shelter’s director thanked the students and promised to send photos of the animals using their new blankets.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the bracketed portion?
options: The students’s goal was to raise enough money to buy new blankets for every dog and cat.
The student’s goal was to raise enough money to buy new blankets for every dog and cat.
The students goal was to raise enough money to buy new blankets for every dog and cat.
The students’ goal was to raise enough money to buy new blankets for every dog and cat.
questions.explanation: The goal belongs to multiple students in the math club, so the plural possessive “students’” is needed. The singular “student’s” would mean that only one student had the goal, while the other choices either omit the possessive marker or add an unnecessary extra s.

questions.passage: Every year, the town of Ashford holds a river cleanup day. Volunteers meet at Riverside Park at 8:00 a.m. and receive gloves, bags, and safety instructions. [The town’s largest employer, Hartwell Manufacturing, donates supplies and gives employees paid time off to participate.] Teams then spread out along the riverbank to collect trash. Last year, more than three hundred volunteers removed 1,800 pounds of litter. Organizers hope even more residents will join this year.
questions.q: The writer wants to emphasize the community’s generosity. Which choice best replaces the bracketed sentence?
options: Many volunteers bring their own water bottles and snacks to the cleanup.
Last year, the event ended with a picnic for all participants.
The cleanup is a fun way to spend a Saturday morning outdoors.
The town’s largest employer, Hartwell Manufacturing, donates supplies and gives employees paid time off to participate.
questions.explanation: The sentence about Hartwell Manufacturing directly shows generosity by describing donated supplies and paid time off for employees to volunteer. The other choices describe participants’ habits, recreation, or a picnic but do not focus on generosity. Keeping the original sentence best supports the writer’s goal.

questions.passage: Every Saturday morning, volunteers at the Riverbend Community Pantry sort donated food into categories before it reaches the shelves. [They separate canned vegetables from canned fruit, check expiration dates, and place damaged items in a return bin.] Teens from the nearby high school often work alongside retired neighbors, and the shared task makes the morning pass quickly.
questions.q: The writer wants to focus this paragraph on the specific steps volunteers take to organize donations. Should the writer keep or delete the bracketed sentence?
options: Delete it, because it repeats the idea that volunteers sort donations.
Keep it, because it introduces the volunteers' reasons for joining the pantry.
Keep it, because it names concrete sorting tasks that support the paragraph's focus.
Delete it, because the paragraph does not mention teenagers elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The bracketed sentence gives specific examples of how volunteers sort donations, which is precisely the paragraph's focus. Deleting it would remove concrete details, and the sentence does not merely repeat the opening idea.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The advisory committee [have reviewed] the new attendance policy and plans to present its findings to the principal on Monday. Members want to gather feedback from teachers before the final vote next week. The group has met twice since September to compare attendance data from several schools.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: has reviewed
have reviewed
review
were reviewing
questions.explanation: The subject is committee, a collective noun treated as singular in American English, so it requires the singular verb has reviewed. The singular form also agrees with the later verb plans.

questions.passage: Maya's science fair project [a model of a solar-powered water heater] won first place in the regional competition, earning her a spot at the state fair. Her teacher said the design was especially efficient because it used recycled materials.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the bracketed portion?
options: a model of a solar-powered water heater
, a model of a solar-powered water heater
, a model of a solar-powered water heater,
a model of a solar-powered water heater,
questions.explanation: The phrase a model of a solar-powered water heater renames project and is nonessential, so it should be set off by commas on both sides. Omitting either comma disrupts the sentence.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: Neither of the twins [have completed] the safety training required for the pottery studio, so both must attend Saturday's session before they can use the wheel. The studio's manager said the session will cover clay preparation, kiln rules, and cleanup.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: have completed
were completing
complete
has completed
questions.explanation: Neither is singular, so the verb should be has completed rather than have completed. The present perfect tense also fits the statement about training that remains unfinished.

questions.passage: The student panel will include [Lena Ortiz, a poet from the East Side, Marcus Lee, a robotics captain, and Priya Shah, a water-quality researcher]. Each panelist will answer questions about how young people can start community projects. The event will be held in the school auditorium.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the list in the bracketed portion?
options: Lena Ortiz, a poet from the East Side; Marcus Lee, a robotics captain; and Priya Shah, a water-quality researcher
Lena Ortiz, a poet from the East Side, Marcus Lee, a robotics captain, and Priya Shah, a water-quality researcher
Lena Ortiz, a poet from the East Side; Marcus Lee, a robotics captain, and Priya Shah, a water-quality researcher
Lena Ortiz; a poet from the East Side, Marcus Lee; a robotics captain, and Priya Shah; a water-quality researcher
questions.explanation: Because each panelist is identified by a name and an appositive containing a comma, semicolons are needed to separate the three main list items. A semicolon list uses semicolons between items and before the final and, with none of the internal commas replaced by semicolons.
